title: Census study: AI-exposed college grads face 13% earnings drop
source_used: Census Bureau working paper page CES-WP-26-56 (abstract), Inside Higher Ed (22 Sep 2026), Streamline Feed (12 Oct 2026); Campus Reform was blocked
key_facts: Working paper 'Graduating into Disruption: Labor Market Outcomes for AI-Exposed College Majors', by Cody Orr, Lee C. Tucker and Lawrence Warren, Census Bureau Center for Economic Studies, September 2026.
In regression-adjusted estimates, the most AI-exposed decile of majors saw initial employment likelihood fall by five percentage points and full-quarter initial earnings fall by 13%.
The authors compare the earnings decline to losses from graduating into a large recession.
Roughly half the earnings decline is lower pay within industries; the rest is a shift into lower-wage sectors such as restaurants and retail.
Effects shrink as graduates move further from entry but remain substantial for the most exposed majors.
Inside Higher Ed (22 Sep 2026) lists computer science, accounting, journalism and engineering among the most exposed majors and nursing and education among the least.
The authors say they lack enough data on whether affected graduates recover.
quote_evidence: In regression-adjusted estimates, the most AI-exposed decile of college majors saw their likelihood of initial employment decline by five percentage points, while full-quarter initial earnings declined by thirteen percent.
This earnings decline is comparable in magnitude to the earnings losses associated with graduating into a large recession.
The report identifies graduates who majored in computer science, accounting, journalism and engineering among the most AI exposed.
why_it_matters_hint: A Census Bureau working paper links AI exposure of college majors to weaker first jobs and pay.
notes: Campus Reform article of 16 Oct 2026 could not be read; the finding is about six weeks old.
